questions.question: Why freeze the task record schema before writing scoring code?
options: It locks the contract so metrics, runners, and post-processors agree on field names
It makes the underlying JSON parser execute measurably faster on large task files
It removes the need for a separate validator step later in the pipeline
It allows task authors to add arbitrary new metric names without any further schema changes
questions.explanation: The schema is the contract every downstream consumer reads from. Locking it lets you change components independently without breaking the rest — it has nothing to do with parser speed or validator removal.

questions.question: What is the closed vocabulary that the metric_name field accepts?
options: Whatever string the task runner happens to be configured to recognise at load time
Any string the task author chooses to write into the metric_name field freely
Only exact_match and f1; the other four metric names are reserved for a future lesson
The six pinned names: exact_match, f1, bleu_4, rouge_l, accuracy, and code_exec
questions.explanation: The lesson pins the metric vocabulary to six names. Adding one requires a new lesson and a new validator entry — it is not runner-configured or author-chosen freely.

questions.question: What does the validator do when it sees an unknown top-level field on a record?
options: Strips the unrecognized field silently and continues processing the rest of the record
Returns a validation error and rejects the record outright, without silently accepting it
Logs a warning to stderr but still accepts and continues processing the record as fully valid
Renames the unknown field to metadata.unknown and keeps it as part of the record going forward
questions.explanation: Unknown fields are a forward-compatibility hazard. The validator rejects them so the schema stays the only source of truth — it does not strip, warn-and-accept, or rename.

questions.question: Why are few-shot examples attached to the task record rather than computed by the runner?
options: Because the task runner in this lesson has no file I/O capability and cannot read example files
Attaching the examples directly to the record saves a small amount of disk space overall
Author intent is part of the eval; binding examples to the task removes per-model prompt variance
Few-shot examples are only ever used during a fine-tuning run, never during evaluation
questions.explanation: Few-shot composition is part of the eval definition, not the model interface. Putting it in the task means every model sees the same prompt.

questions.question: Which category-metric pair is illegal under the validator?
options: summary + rouge_l, a pairing the validator accepts since ROUGE is meant for free-text summaries
arithmetic + exact_match, a pairing the validator accepts since arithmetic answers are exact strings
code_exec + code_exec, a pairing the validator accepts since it names the same thing twice
mcq + bleu_4, since scoring a single selected letter with a text-overlap metric is meaningless
questions.explanation: BLEU on a single letter is meaningless. The validator enforces that mcq tasks use exact_match or accuracy only; the other three pairs are all accepted.

questions.question: What does the post_process rule extract_letter return when the generation is `Answer: C is correct`?
options: C — the validator's first character matching the pattern [A-E] found anywhere in the generation
Answer — the validator extracts the preceding word instead of the letter itself
An empty string — because no character in [A-E] appears anywhere in the generation
The full generation string unchanged, since extract_letter found no matching letter pattern
questions.explanation: extract_letter returns the first character matching [A-E] in the generation. The string has C at the start of the body, so it is neither empty nor left unchanged.
